name: Rural Gothic Villa

lineage.note: The architect-designed, large-budget expression of the parent, in which the plan is genuinely irregular rather than ornamentally so.
Direct: Davis and Upjohn worked from Loudon, from Pugin, and from English published villa designs, and Upjohn had trained in England.
Oriels, tracery, label moulds, and clustered stacks quoted from Tudor and Perpendicular domestic work; the plan and the structure owe nothing to it.

description.short: The full-dress Gothic Revival country house: an architect-composed, genuinely irregular villa of towers, oriels, clustered chimneys and unequal gables, sited to be read in silhouette against trees and sky.
description.long:
The Rural Gothic villa is the American picturesque at full budget, and it is where the movement's ideas were worked out before being cheapened for the mass market. Alexander Jackson Davis established the type at Glen Ellen in 1832 and perfected it at Lyndhurst in 1838; Richard Upjohn built the wooden version at Kingscote in 1839; Downing published, praised, and theorised them. The essential move is that the plan is irregular for real reasons, a library wing where the morning light is, a veranda where the river view is, a service ell turned away from the approach, and the elevation is then composed to make that irregularity look inevitable rather than accidental.

It sits at an interesting technological angle to the rest of this branch. Balloon framing and machine ornament are what made the cheap Carpenter Gothic cottage possible, but the villa often refuses both: Lyndhurst is marble, Kingscote is timber with hand-worked detail, and the ambition of these houses reaches back toward the craft economy the rest of the century was leaving. What the villa does share with its cheaper sibling is total dependence on the pattern book for distribution. Davis drew a few dozen villas; Downing printed them; and within fifteen years there were Rural Gothic villas from Maine to Michigan built by men who had never met either of them. The book, not the guild, is the transmission organ of the entire American picturesque, and that is the historically closest analogue to what a machine-readable design language is attempting.

Downing's moral case is at its most explicit here, and it should be read as a serious position and not as decoration. He held that the villa of a cultivated family ought to express individuality, domestic affection, and a settled relation to its landscape; that a symmetrical facade lies about a household, since no family lives symmetrically; that the veranda is a moral instrument because it mediates between the private hearth and the public sublime of the American landscape; and that a house built on these principles would improve the people in it and, by demonstration, the neighbours around it. He also, more shrewdly, argued that the villa should look as though it had grown, which supplied a permission structure for the additive plan that American families needed anyway.

The experience is one of continuous rearrangement. There is no single correct view of a Rural Gothic villa; move twenty feet along the drive and a different gable dominates, the tower swings behind a chimney stack, the oriel catches the light. The silhouette is doing all the work, and it was designed to be read at a distance through trees. Come inside and the drama collapses into intimacy: a low entrance hall, a stair with a moulded rail and pierced brackets, a library with a bay looking down the slope, dark woodwork, small panes, and a general sense of being pleasantly and deliberately enclosed. Davis understood that the picturesque house must be exciting outside and quiet inside, and the ones that fail usually fail by reversing that.

defining_characteristics: A genuinely irregular plan, with wings, ells, and bays generated by room use and orientation rather than by facade composition
Three or more gables of unequal width forming a hierarchical silhouette against the sky
Steep pitches of 12:12 or greater throughout, with the roof reading as the dominant mass
Clustered, diagonally set, or moulded chimney stacks carried well above the ridge and composed as part of the outline
Oriel or bay windows on the principal rooms, with label mouldings and tracery heads
A veranda, loggia, or cloister of substantial depth attached to at least one principal elevation
Ornament worked in the building's own material, whether stone, stucco, or timber, rather than sawn and applied
diagnostic_tells: The plan is irregular, not merely the ornament. Walk the building; if the footprint has fewer than six external corners it is a Carpenter Gothic cottage wearing villa clothes
No two gables are the same width; equal gables indicate a builder's composition
Chimneys are designed objects with expressed flues, octagonal or clustered shafts, and moulded caps
Tracery has real depth and profile, cut in stone or in thick timber, and casts a modelled shadow rather than a flat one
There is a designed approach: the drive arrives obliquely so the house is first seen as a corner composition, never head-on

distinguished_from.difference: Architect versus builder, irregular plan versus symmetrical body, ornament in the material versus ornament sawn from board. Cost separates them by an order of magnitude and it shows in the depth of every profile.

The same clients, architects, and picturesque theory, opposite geometry. The Italianate villa is low-pitched, wide-eaved and bracketed with a square campanile; the Gothic villa is steep, bargeboarded, and towered with an octagonal or buttressed turret.

Baronial derives from actual surviving Scottish tower houses and keeps crow-stepped gables, corbelled bartizans, and conical turrets; the Rural Gothic villa derives from English ecclesiastical and Tudor domestic sources filtered through Loudon and Downing.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Silhouette hierarchy. The design is fixed in outline first, against a horizon: one dominant gable, subordinate gables at distinct widths, tower or chimney group completing the profile. Elevations are resolved afterwards, and are permitted to disagree with one another.
typical_ratios: Dominant gable width 1.4 to 2.2 times the next largest gable; equal widths are a failure
Tower or turret rising 0.75 to 1.5 storeys above the main ridge
Chimney stacks 4 to 8 ft above the ridge, with each flue expressed as a separate shaft
Veranda depth 8 to 12 ft, at least 0.35 of the elevation length it serves
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Non-repeating. Openings are placed by room requirement; two windows on one elevation may differ in width, head height, and sill height without fault.

massing_affinities.note: In the Gothic case the tower is octagonal, buttressed, or battlemented rather than a square campanile.
Where the villa grows a service ell in the New England manner.
Too regular; it produces a Carpenter Gothic house rather than a villa.

constraints.statement: The composition shall present not fewer than three gables of distinct width, with the dominant gable at least 1.4 times the width of the next largest. Equal gables are forbidden.
All principal roof pitches shall be 12:12 or steeper, and every pitch on the building shall be within 2:12 of every other. Mixing a steep front gable with a shallow rear roof is prohibited.

test.note: Tests the pitch floor. 'Every pitch on the building within 2:12 of every other' is a spread-among-an-arbitrary-number-of-roof-planes fact -- the vocabulary's roof_slope_lower_deg/upper_deg only names a single two-plane roof's pair, not a general variance check -- and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Chimney stacks shall rise not less than 4 ft above the adjacent ridge and shall express each flue as a separate shaft or panel. A flush or capped-off stack destroys the silhouette the type depends on.

test.note: Tests the chimney-height minimum. 'Each flue expressed as a separate shaft or panel' has no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: A veranda, loggia, or cloister not less than 8 ft deep shall be attached to at least one principal elevation, covering not less than 35 percent of that elevation's length.

test.note: Tests the veranda/loggia/cloister depth minimum. The requirement that it cover not less than 35 percent of that elevation's length is a coverage-percent fact with no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Tracery, label mouldings, and hood moulds shall be worked in the wall material with a minimum relief of 2 in. Flat sawn-board substitutes place the building in the Carpenter Gothic variant instead.

test.note: Tests the relief minimum. 'Worked in the wall material' versus a flat sawn-board substitute is a material-category fact with no matching variable and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Lyndhurst
exemplars.note: Alexander Jackson Davis, 1838 for William Paulding, greatly enlarged 1864-65 for George Merritt. Tuckahoe marble; the type's defining American statement.

exemplars.name: Kingscote
exemplars.note: Richard Upjohn for George Noble Jones. The wooden cottage-villa; later dining room by Stanford White, 1880-81.

exemplars.name: William J. Rotch Gothic Cottage
exemplars.note: A. J. Davis. Published by Downing as Design XXIV, A Cottage-Villa in the Rural Gothic Style, and thereafter the most copied villa design in America.

sources: Andrew Jackson Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850)
Amelia Peck (ed.), Alexander Jackson Davis, American Architect 1803-1892 (1992)
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: Technology and the Picturesque (1978)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: THE NODE PB-7a NAMED. WP-4.1 recorded that this node was left with NO OPENING-ROLE PACK AT ALL as a direct consequence of the library having nothing that encoded a pointed head, and that is the gap this fills. The villa is the type Downing and Davis wrote the plates for, so every figure in the pack was checked against it first: the two-light casement under a hood mould, the sill low enough for a window seat, the bargeboarded gable repeated in the dormer, the tall clustered stack. facade-picturesque stays in the facade role and is not displaced -- the two packs divide cleanly, one saying where the incident goes and the other what the opening in it is.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the best-fitting node in the whole branch for it: the style's own governing_logic is silhouette hierarchy - 'the design is fixed in outline first, against a horizon: one dominant gable, subordinate gables at distinct widths, tower or chimney group completing the profile' - which is this pack's dominant-mass method stated almost verbatim. Constraint c01 (dominant gable at least 1.4x the next largest, equal gables forbidden) is this pack's subordination rule with the style's own numbers attached.

Judgment binding, and the least comfortable one in this batch: this is an architect-designed, real-budget villa, not a farmer's cottage, so room-vernacular's own authority note (measured from ordinary surviving vernacular building) is a stretch. Bound anyway, over room-harmonic, because the style's own text describes the actual room experience in ordinary rather than treatise terms - 'the rooms are low, small-windowed by later standards, and dim... a general sense of being pleasantly and deliberately enclosed' - with no harmonic ratio or musical-mean language anywhere in the node, and the node's own proportional_system states that elevations (and by extension rooms) 'are resolved afterwards, and are permitted to disagree with one another,' the opposite of a Palladian room-shape discipline. Flagged rather than asserted as confident.

The node that states the hierarchy rule and states it as a prohibition, which is rare in this corpus: 'dominant gable width 1.4 to 2.2 times the next largest gable; equal widths are a failure', and separately 'no two gables are the same width; equal gables indicate a builder's composition'. That last phrase is the argument -- a picturesque silhouette works by having a subject, and three gables at 1, 1 and 1 give the eye nothing to look at first. Read against `styles/jacobean.json`, which ranges its gables symmetrically on purpose: same count, opposite instruction, and the pack's rules say which applies where.

Bound for the bargeboard and the porch, behind `facade-gable` and `opening-pointed`. Worth reading here with this node's own hierarchy rule from the gable pack: the ornament goes where the gables do, and since 'no two gables are the same width', neither should the bargeboards be equally elaborate -- the dominant gable carries the pierced work and the subordinate ones a simpler repeat, which is both the composition and the budget.

Optional. This record's 'oriel or bay windows on the principal rooms, with label mouldings and tracery heads' takes the pack's projection rule, and `opening-mullioned` and `opening-pointed` between them hold what the bay's windows are. The octagonal chimney shafts this node also has are NOT this pack: an octagonal flue is a section rather than a plan geometry, and it was one of the keyword matches that made this item look larger than it is.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes say what it is: Vignola's Ionic in Chambers's forms -- eighteen modules of column, four and a half of entablature, the Attic base, the angular capital, the flat frieze -- and they name its own downstream reach as late Georgian and Adam-period British practice and, through the pattern books, American Federal work. This node names a different source tradition for its forms, and names it as the very thing that separates it from Baronial. Its stated wall vocabulary is tracery, label mouldings and hood moulds worked in the material at 2 in relief; there is no column, order, entablature or pilaster anywhere in the record, and the one occurrence of the word 'order' is 'an order of magnitude' about cost. An Ionic entablature cannot dimension the eave of a house whose pitches run 12:12 to 18:12 and whose verge is bargeboarded.
declined_packs.quote: the Rural Gothic villa derives from English ecclesiastical and Tudor domestic sources filtered through Loudon and Downing
declined_packs.note: Governs 3 slots: cornice, door_surround, frieze. 0 slots lose all dimensioning -- all three pass to palladio-ionic, delivered from english-palladian. So the measured consequence is that this villa's cornice, door surround and frieze are dimensioned by Palladio's Ionic instead of Chambers's. The decline is true of this pack and stops this authority; it does not stop a classical order reaching a Gothic villa, which arrives one layer further up and belongs to whichever pass judges palladio-ionic.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes say it is Palladio's Ionic order quoted from Ware -- a nine-module column, an entablature a fifth of the column divided 4:3:5, an architrave in five with a cimacio, a cornice in seven and three quarters, an Attic base -- that is, a classical order used as the dimensioning authority for the wall and its crowning members. This node's record names its own source tradition and names it as something else entirely: English ecclesiastical and Tudor domestic Gothic filtered through Loudon and Downing, with a verge that is bargeboarded rather than corniced ('the Gothic villa is steep, bargeboarded, and towered with an octagonal or buttressed turret') and a stated wall vocabulary of tracery, label mouldings and hood moulds worked in the material at 2 in relief. There is no column, order, entablature or pilaster anywhere in the record, and its governing_logic resolves elevations after the silhouette and permits them to disagree with one another, which is the opposite of an order governing an eave. This is the same contradiction on which chambers-ionic was declined; that decline's own note recorded that the classical order still reached this villa one layer further up and left palladio-ionic to this pass.
declined_packs.quote: the Rural Gothic villa derives from English ecclesiastical and Tudor domestic sources filtered through Loudon and Downing
declined_packs.note: Governs 3 slots on this node: cornice, door_surround, frieze. 0 slots lose all dimensioning -- all three fall through to palladio-tuscan, delivered from italian-renaissance at a further cascade depth. So the measured consequence is that a Gothic villa's cornice, door surround and frieze are dimensioned by Palladio's Tuscan instead of his Ionic; the decline stops this authority and does not, by itself, stop a classical order reaching the node. There is no direct lineage edge between rural-gothic-villa and english-palladian; the delivery is cascade depth 7. No live gate is armed either way.
